- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	\section{Beam Search Compatibility}
2	\label{app:beam-search}
3	
4	OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.
5	The main experiments (\S\ref{sec:experiments}) use greedy decoding; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling} validates nucleus sampling.
6	Here we verify compatibility with beam search, completing coverage of the three standard decoding strategies.
7	
8	\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
9	Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
10	(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
11	Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
12	(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
13	Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
14	Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.
15	
16	\paragraph{Results.}
17	Table~\ref{tab:beam-search} compares beam search ($k{=}4$, \texttt{early\_stopping=True}) against greedy decoding under full S1 constraints across six model-dataset combinations.
18	
19	\begin{table}[h]
20	\centering
21	\small

23	SciERC: 551 documents; DocRED: matched 50-document subsets (same documents for greedy and beam).
24	ET = entity type, RV = relation vocabulary, DR = domain/range, CF = cross-field consistency violation rates (\%); F1 $\times$ 100.}
25	\label{tab:beam-search}
26	\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccccc@{}}
27	\toprule
28	\textbf{Model / Dataset} & \textbf{Decoding} & ET & RV & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
29	\midrule
30	\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551)}
31	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
32	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.53} & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
33	\midrule
34	\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / DocRED (50)}
35	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 8.69 & 2.08 & 59.08 & 8.33 \\
36	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.55} & 58.64 & 9.37 \\
37	\midrule

39	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.08 & 6.56 & 23.49 & 2.54 \\
40	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.93} & 25.04 & 3.33 \\
41	\midrule

53	\bottomrule
54	\end{tabular}
55	\end{table}
56	
57	\paragraph{Discussion.}
58	For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.
59	On SciERC, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (0.93\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (0.08\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and substantially reduces CF (Qwen: 9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.53\%; Llama: 6.56\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
60	On DocRED (matched 50-document subsets), beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (8.69\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (1.58\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with CF reductions of 74\% and 86\% respectively.
61	Llama DocRED shows the largest R-F1 gain ($+$3.4\,pp), consistent with beam search recovering valid type assignments that greedy decoding missed due to constraint fallback.
62	The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.
63	
64	Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
65	On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
66	On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
67	This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters $G(t) \cap S(t) = \emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.
68

85	\bottomrule
86	\end{tabular}
87	\end{table}

89	DR elimination at $k{\geq}4$ confirms that constraint-search failure is resolved with moderate exploration width.
90	CF continues to decrease with larger beam (0.08\% at $k{=}8$, only 2 residual violations), while entity extraction quality improves monotonically.
91	$k{=}4$ represents the optimal cost-effectiveness trade-off: it eliminates all DR violations at roughly half the compute cost of $k{=}8$.
92	
93	\paragraph{Beam width--latency Pareto analysis (LoRA).}
94	% exp_id: d066_beam_sweep
95	Figure~\ref{fig:beam-pareto} and Table~\ref{tab:beam-sweep} extend the beam width analysis to LoRA fine-tuning, where the constrained--unconstrained interaction shifts qualitatively: LoRA + S1 already achieves DR=0\% at $k{=}1$ (greedy), so beam search targets CF reduction rather than DR elimination (contrast: zero-shot requires $k{\geq}4$ for DR=0\%).
96	Among constrained configurations, $k{=}2$ is Pareto optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.39$\times$ latency); $k{\geq}4$ yields diminishing F1 returns with increasing latency (1.63--2.03$\times$).
97	
98	\begin{figure}[h]
99	\centering
100	\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/beam_pareto.pdf}
101	\caption{Latency--R-F1 Pareto frontier for beam search under LoRA fine-tuning (Qwen3-8B, SciERC, 551 documents). Constrained decoding achieves DR=0\% at all beam widths; the star marks the Pareto-optimal configuration ($k{=}2$, constrained).}
102	\label{fig:beam-pareto}
103	\end{figure}
104	
105	\begin{table}[h]
106	\centering
107	\small
108	\caption{Beam width sweep on SciERC (Qwen3-8B LoRA, 551 documents). \textsc{unc}: unconstrained; \textsc{con}: schema-constrained. Latency relative to $k{=}1$ unconstrained. Highlighted row: Pareto-optimal configuration.}

110	\begin{tabular}{@{}cl cccc cc@{}}

113	\midrule

124	 & \textsc{con} & 67.22 & 43.60 & \textbf{0} & 0    & 4.069 & 1.63$\times$ \\

134	Under greedy decoding, the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints already achieves DR=0\% but retains CF=1.18\% (21 cross-field violations across 551 documents), with E-F1=67.05 and R-F1=43.77.

168	Qwen3-8B achieves DR=0\% with near-zero CF (0.01\%); R-F1 is preserved ($\pm$0.06\,pp).

  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & 13.79 & \textbf{0.57} & 26.66 & 4.37 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / DocRED (50)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 28.37 & 0.34 & 51.60 & 4.19 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{21.37} & \textbf{0.19} & 51.78 & 5.70 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Discussion.}
For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.
On SciERC, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (0.93\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (0.08\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and substantially reduces CF (Qwen: 9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.53\%; Llama: 6.56\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
On DocRED (matched 50-document subsets), beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (8.69\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (1.58\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with CF reductions of 74\% and 86\% respectively.
Llama DocRED shows the largest R-F1 gain ($+$3.4\,pp), consistent with beam search recovering valid type assignments that greedy decoding missed due to constraint fallback.
The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.

Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters $G(t) \cap S(t) = \emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.

\paragraph{Beam width ablation.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-ablation} varies beam width $k \in \{1,2,4,8\}$ on Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551 documents) under full S1 constraints.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Effect of beam width on constraint satisfaction and extraction quality (Qwen3-8B, SciERC, 551 documents, full S1 constraints). $k{=}1$ corresponds to greedy decoding.}
\label{tab:beam-ablation}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rcccc@{}}
\toprule
$k$ & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
1 (greedy) & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
2          & 0.35 & 4.12 & 31.54 & \textbf{8.75} \\
4          & \textbf{0}    & 0.53 & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
8          & \textbf{0}    & \textbf{0.08} & \textbf{32.18} & 8.39 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

DR elimination at $k{\geq}4$ confirms that constraint-search failure is resolved with moderate exploration width.
CF continues to decrease with larger beam (0.08\% at $k{=}8$, only 2 residual violations), while entity extraction quality improves monotonically.
$k{=}4$ represents the optimal cost-effectiveness trade-off: it eliminates all DR violations at roughly half the compute cost of $k{=}8$.

\paragraph{Beam width--latency Pareto analysis (LoRA).}
% exp_id: d066_beam_sweep
Figure~\ref{fig:beam-pareto} and Table~\ref{tab:beam-sweep} extend the beam width analysis to LoRA fine-tuning, where the constrained--unconstrained interaction shifts qualitatively: LoRA + S1 already achieves DR=0\% at $k{=}1$ (greedy), so beam search targets CF reduction rather than DR elimination (contrast: zero-shot requires $k{\geq}4$ for DR=0\%).
Among constrained configurations, $k{=}2$ is Pareto optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.39$\times$ latency); $k{\geq}4$ yields diminishing F1 returns with increasing latency (1.63--2.03$\times$).

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/beam_pareto.pdf}
\caption{Latency--R-F1 Pareto frontier for beam search under LoRA fine-tuning (Qwen3-8B, SciERC, 551 documents). Constrained decoding achieves DR=0\% at all beam widths; the star marks the Pareto-optimal configuration ($k{=}2$, constrained).}
\label{fig:beam-pareto}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Beam width sweep on SciERC (Qwen3-8B LoRA, 551 documents). \textsc{unc}: unconstrained; \textsc{con}: schema-constrained. Latency relative to $k{=}1$ unconstrained. Highlighted row: Pareto-optimal configuration.}
\label{tab:beam-sweep}
\begin{tabular}{@{}cl cccc cc@{}}
\toprule
$k$ & Mode & E-F1 & R-F1 & DR (\%) & CF (\%) & Latency (s) & Rel.\ Lat. \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{1}
 & \textsc{unc} & 66.88 & 42.95 & 2.11 & 0    & 2.494 & 1.00$\times$ \\
 & \textsc{con} & 66.88 & 42.95 & \textbf{0} & 0.50 & 2.932 & 1.18$\times$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{2}
 & \textsc{unc} & 67.79 & 44.75 & 1.54 & 0    & 2.954 & 1.18$\times$ \\
 & \cellcolor{blue!8}\textsc{con} & \cellcolor{blue!8}67.71 & \cellcolor{blue!8}\textbf{44.60} & \cellcolor{blue!8}\textbf{0} & \cellcolor{blue!8}0.11 & \cellcolor{blue!8}3.463 & \cellcolor{blue!8}1.39$\times$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{4}
 & \textsc{unc} & 67.49 & 43.72 & 1.89 & 0    & 3.485 & 1.40$\times$ \\
 & \textsc{con} & 67.22 & 43.60 & \textbf{0} & 0    & 4.069 & 1.63$\times$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{8}
 & \textsc{unc} & 66.40 & 43.17 & 1.77 & 0    & 4.194 & 1.68$\times$ \\
 & \textsc{con} & 66.36 & 43.65 & \textbf{0} & 0    & 5.058 & 2.03$\times$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
Under greedy decoding, the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints already achieves DR=0\% but retains CF=1.18\% (21 cross-field violations across 551 documents), with E-F1=67.05 and R-F1=43.77.
Adding beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all residual CF violations (1.18\%\,$\to$\,0\%), yielding zero violations across all four metrics (ET=0\%, RV=0\%, DR=0\%, CF=0\%) while preserving extraction quality (E-F1=66.88, R-F1=43.60; changes within $\pm$0.5\,pp).
Llama-3.1-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints and beam search ($k{=}4$) likewise achieves zero violations across all four metrics (ET=0\%, RV=0\%, DR=0\%, CF=0\%) with R-F1=46.18; the zero-violation result thus generalizes across calibrated model families.
% exp_id: q1_llama_ft_beam_scierc
The three constraint mechanisms (grammar masking, semantic domain-range filtering, and beam exploration) are thus fully composable: each addresses a distinct violation source without interfering with the others or degrading task performance.

Beam search on DocRED (zero-shot, 50 documents) introduces a modest increase in parse failures (3/50, 6\%) compared to greedy (1.1\%), as longer beam-generated sequences occasionally produce malformed JSON in complex documents.
With DR=0 in 50 DocRED documents for both calibrated models, the Clopper-Pearson 95\% CI upper bound is 5.8\%; the full-scale LoRA evaluation below (998 documents, CI${\approx}$0.3\%) provides stronger statistical confirmation.

Table~\ref{tab:beam-docred-lora} reports LoRA + beam-4 results on the full DocRED dev set (998 documents), extending the fine-tuning composability evaluation from SciERC to the higher-$\bar{\kappa}$ regime.
Parse failure rates under LoRA beam-4 range from 1.3\% to 3.5\%, lower than the zero-shot rate.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{LoRA greedy vs.\ beam search ($k{=}4$) on DocRED (998 dev documents) under full S1 constraints.
ET = entity type, RV = relation vocabulary, DR = domain/range, CF = cross-field violation rates (\%); PF = parse failure rate (\%); F1 $\times$ 100.}
\label{tab:beam-docred-lora}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llccccccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Decoding} & ET & RV & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ & PF \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B}
  & Greedy con & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0.22 & 81.87 & 40.79 & 8.5 \\ % d065_qwen_greedy_4096_r2
  & Beam-4 con & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0} & 0.01 & 84.00 & 44.46 & 2.9 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B}
  & Greedy con & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0.26 & 84.71 & 44.70 & 2.6 \\ % d065: 4096 context
  & Beam-4 con & 0 & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{85.23} & \textbf{47.17} & \textbf{1.3} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Llama-3.1-8B achieves zero violations across all four metrics (ET, RV, DR, CF = 0\%) on DocRED with LoRA + beam-4, extending the zero-violation result from SciERC to the high-$\bar{\kappa}$ regime.
Qwen3-8B achieves DR=0\% with near-zero CF (0.01\%); R-F1 is preserved ($\pm$0.06\,pp).
Combined with the sampling robustness results (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling}), these findings confirm that OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is compatible with greedy, sampling, and beam search decoding without modification to the core constraint logic.

\paragraph{Latency overhead.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-latency} reports wall-clock latency for greedy and beam search ($k{=}4$) under LoRA fine-tuning.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{s/doc} & \textbf{Overhead} \\
\midrule
Greedy unconstrained   & 2.612 & 1.00$\times$ \\
Greedy constrained (S1)& 2.873 & 1.10$\times$ \\
Beam-4 unconstrained   & 3.446 & 1.32$\times$ \\
Beam-4 constrained (S1)& 4.013 & 1.54$\times$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Latency per document (SciERC, 551 docs, Qwen3-8B LoRA FT, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell). Overhead relative to greedy unconstrained.}
\label{tab:beam-latency}
\end{table}

Beam search itself adds 32\% latency (4 beams); constraint overhead increases from 10\% (greedy) to 16.5\% (beam) because each beam independently maintains grammar and semantic state.
The total 1.54$\times$ overhead is acceptable for offline batch IE; \texttt{early\_stopping} limits additional compute to partial-sequence exploration.

We also explored a type-consensus constraint that forces identical entity types across all relations within a document.
However, CF violations occur precisely where the consensus type conflicts with domain-range constraints, creating a fundamental CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off.
With DR-aware enforcement (skipping consensus when it would violate domain-range), the layer becomes a no-op (100\% skip rate on 551 SciERC documents and 50 DocRED documents).
This confirms that beam search resolves the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR tension through a fundamentally different mechanism: token-level exploration of paths satisfying both constraints simultaneously.

Semantic-only reduces DR by only 24\% and cannot eliminate RV or ET; this is the \emph{enabling dependency}: adding the grammar layer yields a further 92\% reduction (11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).

\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2.}
S2 achieves comparable DR (0.97\%) but lower R-F1 (8.03 vs.\ 8.36) with fewer triples (1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729) and does not resolve the CF trade-off (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%); we adopt S1 as the primary configuration.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
\label{sec:composability}
Fine-tuning alone reduces DR to 1--2\% but leaves residual violations that vary by schema tightness (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
On SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$), adding S1 eliminates or near-eliminates DR (DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\%): Qwen 1.95\%\,$\to$\,0\%, Llama 1.11\%\,$\to$\,0.09\%, with R-F1 within $\pm$0.1\,pp.
On DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$, 96 relations), S1 eliminates DR: Qwen 0.56\%\,$\to$\,0\% and Llama 0.49\%\,$\to$\,0\%; R-F1 changes are $-$0.10\,pp and $+$0.15\,pp.
Across all four model-dataset settings, DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp.
CF interference drops from $+$9.82\,pp (zero-shot SciERC) to $+$1.18\,pp (fine-tuned), tracing to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X ambiguity (Appendix~\ref{app:cf-distribution}); the semantic layer alone accounts for 39--69\% of DR reduction under fine-tuning (\S\ref{sec:composition}).
LoRA + greedy S1 is the recommended fast deployment configuration: DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\%, CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\% at R-F1 40--46, with $+$10\% latency overhead (\S\ref{sec:runtime}).
Beam search ($k{=}4$) with LoRA eliminates all four violation types on SciERC for both Qwen and Llama (R-F1 43.60, 46.18; \S\ref{sec:beam-results}).

For MF2 on the κ̄ metric, reframing it as a descriptive measure that correlates with enforcement outcomes rather than claiming it's an analytical framework is straightforward and accurate—that's a simple terminology fix.

On MF3 and the pumping lemma proof, the intuition about PDAs being unable to track unbounded entity-type bindings is sound. A PDA's finite stack alphabet limits how many distinct entity-type bindings it can track simultaneously, but in an IE document the number of such bindings can grow arbitrarily large.

The pumping argument follows naturally: when a PDA processes a sufficiently long output with many distinct entities, it must repeat a stack configuration, and pumping at that repetition point can introduce type inconsistencies the PDA can't catch. A half-page appendix proof is tight but feasible.

For MF4, the WikiEvents fine-tuning on just 20 documents is legitimately small, so bootstrap confidence intervals are essential. I can compute those using the existing evaluation data without much overhead.

On SF1, comparing IterGen and PICARD makes sense—

that's a manageable addition. For SF2, I'm uncertain about BoostCD's code availability, so the Director should check that. If it's available and performs well on SciERC/DocRED, it'd be a strong baseline, but 4-8 GPU hours is tight given the May 25 deadline. Playing it safer, I could cite their reported results and discuss methodology instead. On the model scale claim, I should narrow "any autoregressive LM" to "validated on 7-8B models with preliminary 70B results"—and I think there are some Qwen-70B results already in the project. The abstract needs one sentence on the CF trade-off for transparency, and I should trim it down to just 1-2 key numbers to keep density manageable.

The greedy type assignment in the entity registry is a real limitation, and framing it as a Level 3 non-local constraint is the honest way to present it. I also need to fix the "ontology-agnostic" claim—the system does require some form of type constraints. The DocRED beam search discussion for zero-shot is already in the appendix, so the labeling and representativeness notes there are sufficient.

The framework figure is actually the biggest single improvement I can make. A framework paper with no figures in the main text is a serious presentation gap, and this is doable in 3 hours with the right tools. I need to show the pipeline clearly: ontology feeding into the compiler, which generates grammar EBNF and semantic masks, then at decode time showing how token candidates flow through the grammar layer filter.

For the rebuttal questions, Q1 through Q5 are all well-prepared, and the explanation for Q5 about why S2 DR outperforms S1 is correct—it's pipeline error propagation. Now I'm thinking through what data I actually need for Q1 on the fallback cascade analysis. The constrained decoding outputs have per-document predictions, and the constraint failure percentage already captures when fallbacks happen. For a deeper analysis, I'd need the per-triple constraint decision logs showing whether grammar passed, whether semantic passed, and whether fallback occurred. These might be in the inference logs rather than just the output files, or I could re-run a small subset with verbose logging if they're not already captured.

Alternatively, I can work with what I have—the constraint failures themselves are the fallback cases, so I can count how many triples triggered fallback versus the total, then compare whether fallback-triples have different F1 scores than non-fallback ones.

For Q2 on BoostCD code availability, I don't have reliable information and would need to search for it, but citing the reported numbers is the safer approach given the timeline.

On Q3 about the pumping lemma direction, the argument holds: context-free grammars generate strings through a pushdown automaton with a finite stack alphabet, but tracking entity-to-type consistency requires remembering O(|entities|) bindings. When documents have more distinct entities than the stack alphabet can represent, the PDA can't distinguish all binding states, so some inconsistent type assignments will slip through.

The semantic layer is what fixes this—it uses an explicit registry instead of relying on the stack.

For the framework figure, I should show the fallback path where the grammar and semantic constraints don't overlap, forcing a fallback to grammar-only with its CF risks, plus the compile-time versus runtime distinction and a concrete example like the "Task" entity with "Used-for" relations showing which tokens get masked.

## Fallback Cascade Analysis: Data Availability Assessment

### 1. Two Distinct Fallback Mechanisms

The `type_mask_processor_cf_fallback.py` on westd-16980 implements two fallback types:

**A. Grammar-first fallback (G∩S=∅)**: When semantic mask's allowed types have no overlap with grammar-valid tokens (all allowed type tokens already have logits below `_GRAMMAR_MASK_THRESHOLD = -1e8`), the semantic mask is skipped entirely and grammar controls token selection. Tracked via class-level counter `grammar_first_fallback_count`.

**B. CF registry-consistent fallback**: When an entity's registered type from the entity section conflicts with domain/range constraints, the system forces the registered type (cross-field consistency overrides D/R). Tracked via instance-level counter `_cf_fallback_count`. Lines 332 and 376 log these per head_type and tail_type positions respectively.

### 2. What Data Currently Exists

**Aggregate runtime stats** (from `get_fallback_stats()` class method):
- `w1_cf_fallback_scierc_pilot_fallback_stats.json`: 6,237 grammar-first fallbacks out of 17,024 mask calls (36.6%), 763 CF registry fallbacks (4.5%)
- `w5_lora_scierc_unconstrained_eval_fallback_stats.json`: all zeros (unconstrained mode, no constraints applied)

**Post-hoc triple-level estimation** (from `estimate_fallback_rate.py` and `sf7_fallback_coverage.py`):
- `fallback_estimation_results.json`: Per-relation fallback rates for both Qwen DocRED (10.2% of triples) and Qwen SciERC (0.93%), with up to 10 concrete examples per config including doc_id, relation, head/tail types

- BoostCD is an EMNLP 2025 main conference paper with available code, but it's only evaluated on Wiki-cIE and REBEL datasets, not on SciERC or DocRED, so adapting it as a baseline would be risky given our timeline constraints.

Now let me compose my comprehensive response to the Director's 5 questions and overall assessment.

### Q1: MF1 fallback cascade analysis feasibility

YES, partially feasible with existing data:
- Aggregate stats: grammar-first fallback = 36.6% on SciERC (w1_cf_fallback_scierc_pilot_fallback_stats.json)
- Per-relation breakdown from estimate_fallback_rate.py
- Post-hoc estimation can identify which output triples violated D/R constraints (= fallback cases)
- Can cross-reference: do fallback triples have lower F1 than non-fallback triples? YES — just need to join the post-hoc estimation (which triples are fallback) with the eval results (which triples match gold)

NOT feasible without code changes:
- Per-step token-level decision logs
- Distinguishing "fallback triggered but model picked valid type anyway" from "no fallback needed"

Recommendation: The post-hoc analysis is sufficient for the paper. A paragraph quantifying: (1) what % of constraint decisions trigger fallback, (2) what % of output triples are affected, (3) whether fallback triples have different precision/recall. This can be done with existing scripts + a small CPU analysis.

### Q2: BoostCD

Running it as a baseline requires dataset adaptation, which is risky given our deadline.

Recommendation: Cite as related work with methodology comparison only. "BoostCD (Šakota & West, 2025) combines constrained and unconstrained decoding via boosting on Wiki-cIE/REBEL; our approach differs in [X]. Direct comparison is deferred as their evaluation uses different benchmarks."

### Q3: Pumping lemma direction

The direction is correct. A CFG/EBNF can be recognized by a PDA with finite stack alphabet, but cross-field consistency requires tracking entity→type bindings for N entities, which exceeds the stack capacity when N grows large enough.  At that point, the PDA must repeat stack configurations, and pumping at the repeat point can generate strings where an entity has conflicting types across different triples—a violation the PDA can't detect because it can't distinguish between binding states. Half a page should cover this cleanly.

### Q4: Framework figure

The director's suggestion works well. The figure should show compile time on the left with the ontology schema flowing through a compiler to produce EBNF grammar rules and semantic constraint tables, then decode time on the right where each token step combines a grammar mask from XGrammar with a semantic mask from TypeConstraintProcessor to produce the final output mask.

I should highlight the fallback path where the intersection of grammar and semantic masks is empty, forcing a grammar-only fallback that introduces context-free risk. A concrete example would help—something like showing how entity "BERT" typed as "Method" interacts with the relation "Used-for" and its allowed head types.

### Q5: Missing concerns

For the reproducibility commitment, I need to check whether code and data release plans are already mentioned in the paper—if not, this should go in the Limitations or Ethics section. On Table 2, the bootstrap procedure with 10,000 iterations was performed but the confidence intervals aren't displayed in the caption or table itself, which could prompt reviewer questions about where the error bars are.

The post-hoc filtering comparison deserves more prominence—the paper mentions discarding up to 48% of predictions in section 5, but doesn't quantitatively compare this against constrained decoding in the composability table. The key advantage (constrained decoding redirects generation to preserve more valid triples rather than just filtering them out) needs clearer exposition.

For prompt sensitivity, I should verify whether there's an existing analysis in the registry. Looking at the experiments, there does appear to be a prompt sensitivity experiment documented.

Now I'm ready to compile my full response.

2. Cross-field consistency = 追踪 entity→type binding，N 个 entity 需 N 个 mapping
3. N > |Γ|^(stack depth bound) 时，PDA 必须重复 stack configuration

- **左列 Compile-time**：Ontology schema → Compiler → (a) EBNF grammar, (b) Valid-pairs table + Entity type set
- **右列 Decode-time**：每个 token step → G(t) [grammar mask] + S(t) [semantic mask] → G(t) ∧ S(t) → output token
